#8434. No-Oxygen Team Will Try Again on Everest

Last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest. Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and leader Andrei Vasiliev were climbing without oxygen, with no one else on the mountain. Winter is quickly approaching, but they have no intention of going home yet.

“We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast. Still want to try again,” Vasiliev texted to ExplorersWeb over the weekend. The climbers had not intended to reach the summit on that latest attempt up the West Shoulder of Everest via the Lho La Pass. Vasiliev explained that they were not yet acclimatized enough to reach the top without bottled oxygen. They did expect to reach higher than before, but high winds made that impossible.

In a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up. On November 11, the team set off from their tent at the base of the West Ridge, fixing ropes in bitterly cold temperature. Contrary to forecasts, winds were light. The climbers pitched their tent at 6,500m and still had time to fix some ropes above them.

On the following morning, however, the gusts were too strong. After waiting in vain for the gale to abate, and with a forecast of even stronger winds the following day, Kondrashkin returned to the ridge, trying not to be blown away. He advanced between gusts and retrieved his two ice axes and the rope he had left behind the day before. They would need that gear for the descent.

Once at the bivouac, the climbers retrieved their tent, cached some food and fuel, and downclimbed to their Camp 1 at some 5,600m. It lies on the steep section between the Khumbu Glacier and the Lho La. Here, they pitched their tent again.

On Friday, the Russian team rappelled down to the glacier, on a “relatively safe” line to the right, where an avalanche fell as they descended.

Today, the team sits at their lodge in Lobuche and looks intently at weather forecasts. “We have not yet decided when to return to the mountain,” Vasiliev told Explorersweb. “It’s all about the weather, and the forecasts announce high winds on November 20-21.”

Angela Benavides graduated university in journalism and specializes in high-altitude mountaineering and expedition news. She has been writing about climbing and mountaineering, adventure and outdoor sports for 20+ years.

#8432. Two Borrowed Shotguns, Two Record Bucks, and the Best Opening Morning in Ohio History

Early Black Friday deals are here — Shop hunting gear, fishing tackle, optics, and more!

By Dan Allison as told to Merrill C. Gilfillan

Published Nov 18, 2026 9:30 AM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

This story, “The Luck of Irish Ridge,” appeared in the December 1966 issue of Outdoor Life. While it was an incredible deer, Ohio is an incredible state for big whitetails. Allison’s buck is now ranked 41 among Ohio’s biggest typical bucks.

The 1965 deer season in the hill country of southeastern Ohio was 15 minutes old, but the woods were silent. I was hunkered down with my back against a tree in an open place on the side of a big ridge. The place was too open, but I hadn’t realized that when I sat down there just before the opening hour of 9 o’clock. A deer could see me a mile away, I told myself.

But I didn’t want to risk moving, now that shooting was legal. Anyway, I didn’t know where there was a better stand. So I just sat still, hoping for the best.

It was a clear November morning, frosty but promising to warm up later. Most of the timber on the side of the ridge was oak. That meant acorns, and acorns are likely to mean deer. Maybe I hadn’t picked such a bad spot after all. It was warm and pleasant there in the sun. I’d wait awhile and see what happened.

Suddenly, the stillness was shattered by a shot. A few seconds later another one rapped out. Though I wasn’t sure which direction the shots came from, I decided it was some hunter over the ridge behind me. I didn’t dream what had happened. The woods got quiet again, and then bluejays started to holler on the ridge.

I’d hunted deer only three years before this and was too inexperienced to know what those noisy bluejays meant. I’ll know next time.

The next thing I heard was something moving in the dry oak leaves behind me. It didn’t sound big enough for a deer, but it startled me. I swiveled my head slowly for a look. It seemed to take me an eternity to turn my head and body without making any sudden motions or noise.

Whatever I was hearing kept coming, walking slowly and deliberately. I finally got twisted into position and eased one eye around the trunk of the tree I’d been sitting against.

What I saw then literally took my breath away.

Walking slowly down the slope, only 15 or 20 yards away and coming almost straight toward me, was a giant buck with the biggest rack I’d ever seen. The morning sun glinted on his polished, brown tines, and he looked as if he were wearing the bleached roots of an upturned stump on his head. I didn’t know it then, but I was looking at a whitetail deer that was better than any that had ever been killed in Ohio.

He stopped for a second and looked back up the ridge, the direction he’d come from, and I remember thinking that somebody over there must have spooked him. Then he turned my way and came on, walking calmly and unafraid. To this day, I don’t know why I didn’t have the worst case of buck fever a young deer hunter ever had.

My dad, Don Allison, and I had left home the previous evening and driven to Wellston, where we were to stay for the hunting season with dad’s friend and hunting partner, Jim Arthur. We live near South Solon, in the flat prairie country about 40 miles southwest of Columbus. Dad runs a 232-acre farm on some of the nation’s richest land. He handles a herd of 20 Black Angus cows and their calves and feeds out about 350 hogs a year.

I was 17 years old at the time and a senior at Madison South High School south of London.

I’ve hunted with dad ever since I could carry a gun. We get rabbits, pheasants, and fox squirrels in the farming areas around home, and the last few years we’ve made trips for grouse to the hill country of eastern Ohio. In 1962, dad took me deer hunting for the first time.

The deer season is the only real vacation dad takes. He started hunting deer in 1944, the second year Ohio had an open season, and has missed only one fall since, except for years when the season was closed. But he’s been plagued by hard luck. In almost 20 years of hunting, up to last fall, he’d never killed a deer.

The closest he ever came was getting a shot at a doe, but he confessed that buck fever — if a female deer can give you buck fever — got the best of him that time, and he scored a clean miss. He loves to hunt, though, and has never gotten discouraged.

“I’ll be lucky one of these years,” he always said, not knowing just how lucky.

My record was no better. In three falls of hunting, I hadn’t even seen a deer. But, like dad, I was sure my time would come.

Ohio’s 1965 gun season on deer was a restricted one, varying from region to region according to herd conditions and the management plans of the state game men. In the northwestern counties, level farm country, there was a three-day either-sex season, but hunters had to have in advance a landowner’s written permission to hunt in order to get a deer permit.

In the hill country of southeastern Ohio, where we’ve always hunted, there was a bucks-only season beginning on Monday, November 8, and lasting four days. Hunting hours were from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., and only shotguns loaded with slugs or pumpkin balls were legal, as in the past.

As November drew near, dad and I both developed the usual deer-hunting itch. It’s hard to tell anybody how much our annual whitetail hunt means to us. But for a time, it didn’t look as if either of us could make it. Dad had almost 100 acres of corn to pick. Deer season was about a month earlier than usual, and the picking job would be no more than well started by November 8. If he took time off to go hunting, wintry weather could set in before he finished the corn picking.

“I’m going,” he finally told us, “even if I have to pick corn when the snow’s blowing.”

My problem was basketball — I had a good chance to make the school team. We’d practiced about a week when deer season rolled around, and the rule was that anybody who missed practice unexcused would be dropped from the squad.

It was a fair rule, and I knew going deer hunting wasn’t a valid excuse. If I went, my basketball career would end before it started. But the hunt was too much to pass up.

“If you’re going,” I told dad, “so am I.”

There was one other problem. We both had gun trouble. Dad usually shoots a Model 12 Winchester 12 gauge that he’s had for years. But it was out of order, so he borrowed a 12 gauge Remington autoloader. I was getting ready to buy a new shotgun, so I borrowed a Browning 16 gauge automatic on trial. We’d both be using guns we’d had little chance to get familiar with.

“Well, if we see deer and miss,” dad said with a grin, “at least we’ve got a good alibi.”

Dad hunted for many years in the Shawnee State Forest, along the Ohio River west of Portsmouth. It’s a 60,000-acre tract, rugged and steep, with oak-covered ridges and few roads. It’s easy to get lost there unless you’re familiar with the hills. Other parts of Ohio may have more deer, but many hunters prefer this wild country.

Dad had another reason for hunting there. It was the favorite spot of a good friend of his, Belvin Adams. Adams lived in Wheelersburg, only a short distance away, and he and a party of his friends had hunted the Shawnee for years.

But three years ago, the rubber company Adams works for moved him to Indonesia. Since then, Jim Arthur, who lives in Wellston and had worked with Adams, has invited dad and me to stay at his home and hunt with his party in the Raccoon and Zaleski state forests, in Vinton County. These forests have a combined area of about 30,000 acres, and the timberlands are mixed with some farming acreage, making good deer range. That was where dad and I would go for the 1965 season.

Jim Arthur has a son, Steve, who’s my age and, like me, was a senior in high school then. We have a lot in common, especially our enthusiasm for deer hunting.

We got to Wellston Sunday evening, too late to scout the area we intended to hunt. And Jim Arthur told us that he’d been too busy to do any looking in recent weeks. That meant we’d start cold on opening day, not knowing where deer were hanging out or where their feeding grounds and travel routes were. But at least we’d hunted the general area for three years and knew the lay of the land.

We sat up late that night, as we usually do the night before the season opens, recalling other hunts, laying plans, guessing what kind of luck we’d have. And the longer we talked, the higher our hunting fever mounted.

We turned in finally, got a few hours of sleep, and were up early, checking our equipment and taking care of last-minute details. About 8 o’clock, though we couldn’t start hunting for another hour, we drove out to a long hogback called Irish Ridge, between the Raccoon and Little Raccoon creeks, a few miles southeast of Wellston. We didn’t want another party to beat us to our stands, and we wanted to be set at 9 o’clock in case hunters around us began moving deer.

I followed an abandoned township road that wound along the side of the ridge. Steve was quite a way below me on the slope, his dad was walking the crest of the ridge, and my dad was about halfway down on the other side. A few minutes before 9, I picked the oak-tree stand I described in the beginning and settled down.

I heard the two shots and heard the bluejays yell. Then that huge buck came walking slowly down the ridge.

I eased into shooting position slowly and carefully, and I raised the Browning just as cautiously. The buck took a few more steps, reached the old, leaf-strewn road, and stopped to look around. He was only 30 feet away. I had time to remind myself that I was using an unfamiliar gun and to remember how it worked. I pushed the safety off and leveled on him.

Dad had told me many times to shoot for the spine when my chance came. I remembered that advice now and followed it. My 16 gauge rifled slug smashed through the deer’s backbone just behind the shoulders, and he fell like a ton of bricks. But he pulled himself half up on his forelegs, so I did the second thing dad had always instructed me to do.

“Once you get a deer down,” he’d said, “shoot for the heart and finish him in a hurry.”

Dad had read a lot about deer hunting and talked with many hunters, and it never occurred to me that there was anything strange about his having such firm opinions, even though he’d never killed a deer. His advice proved itself again now. I put in a heart shot, and this time the buck didn’t get up.

He was still thrashing around, though, working himself downhill. And suddenly I saw that he was going to fall over a low cliff. I watched, and my heart sank as he rolled over the edge and disappeared. The cliff muffled his fall, and I ran to the edge, almost afraid to look. If part of that magnificent rack had broken, I’d be sick.

He lay dead at the foot of the cliff, 20 or 30 feet below. One front leg, broken in the fall, stuck out at an angle. I couldn’t see enough of his horns to tell about them.

I waited long enough to be sure he was dead and then found a place where I could climb down. I took a good look at his head and breathed a gusty sigh of relief. Not a single point was damaged. Was I thankful!

After my heart stopped thumping, I started wondering how we’d ever get him up to the old road. We couldn’t take him up the cliff, and there was a very steep grade wherever I looked. But before I had time to think much, I heard Steve call. I yelled back, and in a few minutes he joined me. When he saw what I’d shot, he was about as excited as I was, and I guess I was as proud as anybody in Ohio right then.

I had never dressed a deer, so I asked Steve to stay with the buck while I went to find dad. I climbed to the top of the ridge and, before going much farther, heard voices down in a brushy gully. I shouted.

“Come on down,” dad said. When I got there, he and Jim were standing over a mighty big buck, and dad had the happiest look on his face that I’d ever seen.

He had killed his deer almost exactly as I’d taken mine and not more than five minutes earlier. The two shots I’d heard were his.

He’d walked in along the side of the ridge and found the kind of stand he was looking for. He was about to sit when he heard something rustling the dry leaves behind him. When he turned around, there came a big buck, walking downhill toward him.

The deer didn’t see him, and dad waited until it was abreast of him and only 40 feet away. Then he floored it with a spine shot. After falling, it slid down into a gully and out of sight. Dad ran up to the edge and saw that the deer was still kicking, so he finished it off with a slug through the heart.

“I got one the same way over on the other side of the ridge,” I blurted out. Then I took another look at dad’s buck and added, “Only mine’s bigger.”

We shook hands and thumped each other on the back, and I don’t believe there were ever two happier hunters in the deer woods. After 20 years of waiting and trying for dad, and four for me, it was hard to believe that we’d killed two bucks, both big busters, in the first half hour of the season, within a few hundred yards of each other, and with borrowed guns. What luck!

As far as we’ve been able to find out, we were the first father-and-son team ever to take two record-book trophies — both of our bucks turned out to be that — in a single season anywhere in the country, to say nothing of getting them in such a hurry. Those certainly were 20 magic minutes.

Jim and dad had been trying to figure out a way to hang dad’s buck. With three pairs of hands to hoist and heave, it wasn’t too hard. As soon as it was done, Jim started back with me to dress my deer while dad went to work on his.

We found we couldn’t hang my buck. The slope was too steep, and there were no suitable trees. But Jim, Steve, and I pulled and skidded it around so that the head was uphill. Then Jim showed me how to field-dress a deer where it lay.

Four other men, friends of Jim’s and dad’s, had started out to hunt with us that morning. Three of them were nearby, heard us yelling, and came to help. We needed them. Even with part of the crew pulling on ropes and the rest lifting and pushing, it was all the seven of us could do to get my buck up the slope to the old road.

We left him there, went after dad’s, and skidded it to the ridge top. Then we dragged the two bucks out to the cars. It was past noon when we finished and headed to town for lunch.

We hung our two deer side by side in Jim Arthur’s yard. Cars drove by in a steady stream the rest of the day as word of our trophies got around Wellston. Dad phoned home, and mother and Joan Mace, wife of a neighboring farmer, agreed to drive down in the Mace pickup and take the deer home.

By the time they got to the Arthur home, there was so much traffic around it that they had to park two blocks away. We cleared a path through the traffic, loaded the deer, and drove back to the state checking station for the required check.

The bucks were weighed the next morning. Field-dressed, with heart and lungs out, mine tallied 253 pounds, dad’s 240. According to the conversion table we used to estimate their live weight, mine would have gone just over 300 when I shot it, dad’s almost 290.

We took the heads to Max Shipley, a Columbus taxidermist. The minute he saw them, he phoned Merrill Gilfillan of the Ohio Division of Wildlife, to whom I have related this story. Merrill is an official scorer for both the Buckeye Big Bucks Club and the Boone and Crockett Club.

Both were typical-whitetail racks, and to our delight both made the record lists of both clubs. After the required 60-day shrinkage period, mine scored a whopping 187 6/8, dad’s 160 2/8. Up until this point, we hadn’t realized how big our bucks really were.

According to the 1964 edition of the Boone and Crockett Club’s Records of North American Big Game, mine is the biggest typical whitetail ever killed in Ohio and rates a place among the first 10 on the list. I have entered it in the 1966-67 Boone and Crockett competition. Officials tell me that any deer scoring that high has a very good chance of winning first place among typical whitetails in that competition.

For some reason, Ohio produces far more than its fair share of big whitetail heads. It’s by no means one of the big deer-kill states. The herd numbers only an estimated 20,000 to 30,000, and in recent years hunters have killed fewer than 1,000 annually, as compared with kills of 100,000 and more in such leading whitetail states as Minnesota, Michigan, and Wisconsin.

Yet there has been no recent season that did not see three to five Ohio bucks make the Boone and Crockett record list in either the typical or nontypical category. In six open seasons between 1956 and 1962 (deer hunting was closed in 1961), 24 Ohio deer qualified for that honor, 13 of them typical racks, 11 nontypical.

We shook hands and thumped each other on the back, and I don’t believe there were ever two happier hunters in the deer woods.

And in the 1958-59 big-game competition sponsored by the Boone and Crockett Club, Ohio whitetails — one with a typical rack and the other nontypical — won first place in both those categories.

The nontypical deer was killed in Ashtabula County in 1957 by James L. Clark of Ashtabula, and the typical buck in Harrison County a year later. Dr. James Rumbaugh and John Ruyan of Westerville shared the honors on that one, both having shot at it. Clark, in collaboration with Merrill Gilfillan, told the story of those two busters in “How I Got No. 1 Deer,” in the November, 1960, issue of Outdoor Life.

In addition, about 180 heads have qualified in the last 10 years for a place on the record list of the Buckeye Big Bucks Club, a state organization sponsored by the Division of Wildlife. Minimum score requirement for this club is 140, just 20 points below that of the Boone and Crockett Club.

Game men believe that Ohio’s phenomenal showing is due to a favorable combination of cropland and woodland — providing an abundance of top-quality deer food — plus certain trace minerals in the soil and hunting rules that have prevented both overhunting and overcrowding of the range. Vinton County, for example, where we hunted, is more than two thirds woods and brush but does have some farmland, including cornfields, in the valleys. That’s likely to mean big, healthy deer.

Read Next: The Incredible Hunt for the C.W. Shelton Buck, One of the Widest Bucks in the World

As for the consequences of our hunt, dad fared better than I did. He finished his corn picking in cold weather but without any real problems. But I missed out on something pretty special. Our basketball team turned out to be a championship outfit, winning the Darby Valley League pennant and all but the last game in the district tournament. But I wasn’t on it.

Dad and I were both disappointed about that, but if I were doing it over again, I’d make the same choice. I can’t ever be sorry I went on that deer hunt.

#8430. Officials Blame Climate Change for Glacier Collapse That Killed 17

Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.

A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10. Another 10 were unharmed and made it down the mountain on their own.

The impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them. As we reported at the time, helicopter pilot Alexander Davydov caught the avalanche on video.

Eldar Khashkhozhev of the Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations explained that warmer temperatures melted the protective blanket of snow, exposing parts of the glacier. This weakened the ice support that had glued enormous masses of snow and ice in place for decades.

A helicopter inspection of the region’s snow conditions the month before found no cause for concern, and some officials insist the catastrophe was unpredictable. However, climber Dmitry Polyakov, who was in the region at the time, disputed the idea that the glacier posed no danger. He said climbers had long recognized its instability and generally avoided approaching it in large groups.

The Mizhirgi Glacier against Mizhirgi East and West peaks, site of September’s catastrophic glacial collapse. Photo: Shutterstock

The key points of Khashkhozhev’s explanation were:

Rising temperatures have raised the altitude of permanent snow cover.

Previously protected sections of the glacier became exposed, weakening the supporting ice beneath the hanging masses.

Eventually, gravity overcame that support and triggered a collapse that struck the training group.

This was the largest climbing disaster in the country since 2002, when another glacier collapse in North Ossetia, located between the Black and Caspian Seas, killed 125 people, including local residents.

With major landslides in summer and the possibility of glacial collapse at other times of the year throughout the world, mountaineers will have to adjust their behavior, as previously safe areas become potentially deadly.

#8428. Public-Land Sales, Energy Dominance, and Data Centers: What Interior’s Master Plan Really Means for Outdoorsmen

Early Black Friday deals are here — Shop hunting gear, fishing tackle, optics, and more!

Published Nov 18, 2026 11:00 AM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Less than two months after a dinner at the White House with leaders of hunting and angling groups in which President Trump and Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum confirmed support for conservation priorities, Burgum has formalized the Trump administration’s plans to shrink the federal estate and to site industrial data centers and energy infrastructure on America’s public lands.

As we reported last week, the intentions are outlined in the Department of the Interior’s five-year strategic plan that extends through 2030. The document serves as a blueprint for implementing the priorities of the Bureau of Land Management, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Bureau of Reclamation, National Park Service, and Bureau of Indian Affairs, among other Interior agencies.

The 28-page plan is short on details but long on statements about the department’s role in domestic energy “dominance,” “unleashing the potential” of America’s public lands, and pursuit of “public-private partnerships.” In addition to his role at the helm of the Department of Interior, Burgum also chairs the White House National Energy Dominance Council.

The few detailed directives contained in the five-year plan note Interior’s intention to “decrease the size of the federal estate by offering to states, localities, and Tribes the opportunity to purchase federal lands” in order to better focus the department’s resources on “nationally significant federal lands.” The strategic plan further emphasizes Interior’s pursuit of “strategic rights-of-way agreements, land exchanges, and direct transfer of lands in support of reliable energy production and transport.”

And the plan specifically calls for redirecting revenue from the Land and Water Conservation Fund, which is funded by offshore oil and gas leasing revenue, to private-land easements rather than outright purchase of land by the government for recreation and resource purposes. The fund provides about $900 million annually to acquire land, improve existing properties, and invest in communities’ cultural and outdoor recreation assets.

The Department of Interior’s plan’s mention of possible land sales provoked quick push-back from lawmakers from both parties who recall the tsunami of opposition to inclusion of federal land sales as part of the 2025 Big Beautiful Bill. Language that would have funded tax breaks by selling large parcels of public land was eventually withdrawn from that bill, which was later signed into law by Trump.

Both of Montana’s Republican senators, including retiring Sen. Steve Daines, who sits on the powerful Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, told the news agency Politico that they were not consulted on Interior’s strategic plan and would oppose the idea of land sales. Yesterday, Burgum, responding to growing criticism of the land-sale language, told Fox News that national parks would not be sold. He called public-land supporters’ reaction to the strategic plan “manufactured hysteria.”

But the renewed conversation around the topic, along with the plan’s focus on energy development and investment in “Super Intelligence” infrastructure, raises the question: How seriously should America’s hunters, anglers, and outdoor enthusiasts take Interior’s blueprint, or is the strategic plan simply glossy “shelfware” that will be ignored as a new Congress convenes in January and other priorities shove it to the background?

“The thing about these plans is that they don’t really hold a lot of authority,” says a government affairs executive who didn’t have permission to speak on the record. “The agencies have to put them out periodically, but this is not a chapter-and-verse regulatory document or a change in the statute. Instead, you can read it as a sort of statement of purpose.”

In order to execute sales or transfers of federal land, they note, the Interior would have to undertake a formal land-use planning process with opportunities for public comment. That’s a core provision of the Federal Land Policy and Management Act. But some conservation groups are signaling that a new bill working its way through the lame-duck Congress this week, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would undermine many of those land-disposal requirements. And the administration’s undercutting of the BLM’s Resource Management Plans further weakens norms that have kept land transfers a rare exception.

Related: Senate Poised to Vote on Affordability Bill that Hunters, Anglers Worry Is a Trojan Horse for Public-Land Rollbacks

A more present worry isn’t outright land sales, which are overwhelmingly opposed by America’s hunters and anglers. It’s the long-term lease of federal lands for hyper-scale data centers and energy facilities, says Randy Newberg, a longtime public-land advocate and podcaster.

“Within this vision plan is an awful lot of what I’d call greasing the skids for private development of public land, which in all aspects is quasi-ownership of public land,” says Newberg. “Given the transactional nature of this administration, I worry about sweetheart deals that help your buddy who is friends with the president or cabinet secretary to develop data centers or oil and gas facilities, you name it.”

Newberg says the outcome is the opposite of conservation.

“Under that vision document, you can just about bet that our public lands will become far more industrialized than any of us probably ever expected.”

No one should be especially surprised to see land transfer discussed at this vision-document level. After all, it’s a plank in Republican Party platforms in several states, including Montana, where party leaders last summer amended the position confirming their support for public-land transfer but also encouraging public access.

Montana’s GOP ratified the updated platform in June to read “Support transferring federally managed lands to the state with a transition plan and continued public access.” The previous version had simply encouraged transfer of federal lands to the states “in order to secure statehood equality and provide for better management of public lands.”

Interestingly, even the polarizing Project 2025 document, organized by the Heritage Foundation to prioritize policies of the incoming second Trump administration, doesn’t explicitly advocate transferring federal land. On the other hand, the document’s section outlining Department of the Interior priorities — maximizing energy production on federal lands, rolling back protections for national monuments, and weakening environmental reviews — are all reprised in Burgum’s five-year plan.

One of the few times the current Congress pushed back on administrative priorities in the second Trump term was to remove the land-transfer provisions of the Big Beautiful Bill. That opposition was led by Montana Rep. Ryan Zinke (R), the former Secretary of Interior in Trump’s first term, who later founded the Public Lands Caucus in Congress. But the next Congress, with majority Democrats energized by successes in this month’s mid-term election, is likely to demand oversight and review of federal agencies, including Interior.

One of the incoming freshmen, Democrat Sam Forstag, took Zinke’s western Montana seat by about 9 points. It’s the first time in 30 years that Montanans elected a Democrat to represent them in the U.S. House of Representatives. Forstag is a U.S. Forest Service smokejumper and union leader who ran on issues of affordability and against politics that “puts working people last.”

Speaking from Washington, D.C., yesterday as he rushed between meetings and caucused with fellow freshmen, Forstag says that public-land management has the potential to be a rare bipartisan issue.

“The notion of shrinking the federal estate and selling off our public lands sounds damned concerning to me,” Forstag said. “I think particularly as we’re seeing a change of leadership in Congress, this is the issue I see as having the most potential for not just bringing the [Democrat] caucus together but building bipartisan support. Republicans who may not have stood up publicly when we needed them the last couple of years are coming around that when it comes to actual people, public lands are not a partisan issue. They’re one of the last places where you don’t have to be rich to get access to it. [Public lands] are a reason Montana is a place worth living while costs skyrocket.”

Forstag, who hopes to land an assignment on the House Committee on Natural Resources, says he considers talk about selling or leasing federal lands for data centers or energy infrastructure to be a “distraction.”

Read Next: The Rush to Build Data Centers on Public Lands Is Worse Than You Thought

“The way you fix affordability isn’t selling off what little bit working people still have,” he says. “The way you fix affordability is not building a data center in the wilderness. It’s getting private equity the hell out of housing, and reinvesting in things like Community Development Block Grants, which have been systematically underfunded for decades while billionaires got tax cuts.”

Andrew McKean is Outdoor Life’s hunting and conservation editor, drilling into issues that affect wildlife, wildlands, and the people who care about them. He’s also OL’s optics editor, helping readers to make informed buying decisions.

#8426. Te Araroa: mum, please send me $32

After my very dark dome day, I went to bed feeling proud of myself but worried that I’d wake up feeling equally tired. Much to my delight, however, I slept well and woke up feeling pretty restored. It’s amazing what a shower, some food, and a sleep will do for your body.

Notes from the trail log at the dome cafe (no longer actually a cafe)

We had been discussing “trail legs” for a couple of days now, wondering if maybe we were finally getting them. I think on this day I got my first inkling of them, we walked as a group this morning (except Charlie who we knew would catch up as she’s the fastest out of all of us) and zoomed through the first ten kilometres. It was easy gravel road and the clouds hadn’t burned off yet. I felt good despite how hard I’d found the day before.

Sinèad, Annabel and I stopped for a snack break before the final hill portion of the day. The sun had started to burn off the clouds at this point, and it was starting to get hot. But we knew we only had about 15km into Puhoi (where we’d find food and maybe even a beer), and a campsite in 10km where we could replenish our water. So we pushed on.

This section of the day was a slog, not because the terrain was hard (it was just a gravel road) but because the sun was so hot. Saying we were sweaty would be an understatement, but there was nowhere to stop to cool off because the whole track was exposed. So we pushed on.

At some point Charlie did catch us and we all continued our climb up the gravel hill. This was the moment that I really decided that my merino hoodie was going to have to go. Luckily I have Fraser at home with access to my lighter-weight synthetic sun hoodies so I got him to send one to my friend in Auckland. Feels nice to not have to spend money unnecessarily.

Eventually, like finding an oasis in a desert, we spotted a little side track that led to a grassy, shaded area. I made a beeline for it and dropped all my stuff. It was approaching noon and I decided it was lunch time so took off my sun hoodie and pulled out my remaining trail pizza ingredients. This break was such a relief!

After drinking about half a litre of water and eating my two wraps (this time with added chilli flavoured corn nuts for crunch), I felt fortified enough to keep walking in the sun.

The rest of the afternoon passed in a sweaty blur and soon we found ourselves descending a strange path between two paddocks toward the Remiger road campsite at km 533. At this point I had pretty much run out of water so I powered ahead, focused on the water tank I knew was at the camp. It was a beautiful camp with a nice shelter, and after our 20 very hot kilometres it was a really great place for a break.

We had decided the night before that we’d try to make it into Puhoi and the call of the pub was strong enough to keep us from pitching tents at Remiger road. After a decent, shoe off, stretch out kind of break we were ready to conquer the final 4.5km of road walking.

With eternal hope in our hearts, we gave hitching a go, but people only sped up when they saw us. Thanks, Auckland.

Once we realized that hitching wasn’t going to happen, we began our road walk to Puhoi. It went surprisingly quickly and soon Charlie was dancing and waving her poles out front of the Puhoi tea rooms.

Annabel, Charlie, me and Sinèad at the tea rooms after checking in. Photo courtesy of Sinèad

The tea rooms were our home for the night, for $10 you get a very non-private shower (but there’s hot water so I’m not complaining), wifi, charging, and a tent site. The owner also does a special offer for TA hikers where he re-opens the cafe just for us and will make you anything off the menu or a burger. This seemed much nicer than walking a further 500m to the pub and was probably also cheaper, so we all agreed to stay in for the night.

We also met up with Moritz who had taken a zero at the tea rooms. He was full of energy and went to the shop to buy us snacks and used his flip fuel to top up our gas canisters. Before I left for Te Araroa I told Fraser I was sure I’d meet someone who would be able to do that, and once again: the trail provides.

I went to bed full and happy, and with the knowledge that because of tides, we’d have a very slow morning and then a chill 8km kayak down the Puhoi river the next day.

With our kayaks booked at 1pm, we had a slow morning. I had time to blog, charge all my electronics, dry my tent and order my blasphemous breakfast (see blog post about food for more). It was a luxurious morning and included coffee!!

At about 11:30am we headed toward the pub and general store where I did a small resupply and got some lunch and another coffee. I was not messing around with coffee anymore, not after how I felt on the dome day.

At 1pm, we made our way to the kayak place, got our briefing, and dropped off our packs. The awa (river) is the official TA trail, which is pretty cool! It requires an outgoing tide, so the moon and ocean and river decide what time your day starts. It felt sort of lovely to know that we didn’t have a choice of when we started. The awa has long served as a highway for waka (boats) and its name translates to “slow water”.

The awa is aptly named, and the kayak down it was so peaceful. I spent a lot of time just being carried by the current and paddling intermittently only to steer. Though the highway now runs over and beside the awa, it’s still a lovely space. As I paddled down, I watched the water turn from a murky brown river to clear, salinated ocean water.

A penguin floated past and I desperately tried to point it out for the people behind me. As I approached the end of the river, I spotted rays. It was magical.

Once off the kayaks, everyone agreed that it would be rude not to swim. So we got in the now ocean water. It was refreshing, and so warm compared to the water I’m used to swimming in in Wellington. The ground, however, was a whole strange experience. I spent most of the swim trying to keep my feet from touching the gooey mud on the bottom and Annabel and I screamed as our feet sank in.

Soon we were all back in our dry clothes, socks and dry-ish shoes. We said bye to Anica who was nursing an Achilles injury, which was sad.

There wasn’t much left in the day and we’d have to wait for a tidal section on the other side of a small hill. We set off anyway, and got our legs back into the habit of walking after our lazy morning and kayak.

On top of the hill between the end of the Puhoi and Waiwera

By the time we reached Waiwera (which translates to hot water because of the hot springs in the area) Charlie and I were not feeling keen to wait for the tides. My beach-blisters were hurting and making me feel like I was limping, and Charlie was just generally not feeling well. We decided to split up, and she and I took a bus into Ōrewa to check us all into the campground while the other two waited for the tides.

Charlie on the bus – she has a very similar shot of me

The Ōrewa holiday park was by far the worst place we’ve stayed. The “tent sites” were actually just hard-packed ground with a ton of tree roots. But the staff were really nice and I decided I’d ask at the office how much it would cost to upgrade to a cabin (it ended up being $1.25 extra each). I’m so glad I did!! There were some strange characters at the park and one guy told us that his laundry had been stolen the night before, so it felt nice to have a lock on the door.

Our little cabin was soon full of tents drying out, and dry bags jammed into every corner. We pondered whether we could fit Moritz in on the floor but luckily another hiker, Tim, had booked the cabin beside ours so he got a real bed.

I was happy to leave Ōrewa, and knew we were heading for a big supermarket and shopping mall. The walk this morning was easy and quick into Silverdale, where we all split up to run our respective errands. I spent way too much money buying blister plasters and restocking my supplements at chemist warehouse, but offset that by NOT buying a pastry at the coffee shop.

Caffeinated and ready to go, we packed up our new things and started the walk to Stillwater. This was all road and started relatively pleasantly with wide sidewalks and grassy shoulders. But eventually we got on the final stretch of road to Stillwater and it became the worst road we had encountered on the whole trail so far. Big trucks blasted past us and we scrambled to not fall into the steep ditches. When we finally came to a spot where someone could pick us up, Annabel, Sinèad and I decide to try to hitch.

Charlie, being ever the bravest of us, continued along the road and said the road did eventually get better.

A lovely couple picked us up and started telling us about a cabin we could stay in along the Ōkura walkway. This led to them calling their daughter who said that the cabin was SO FAR into the walk, like thirty minutes. We all laughed out loud at that and then she asked her mum to send her $32. Walking the bulk of that scary road was made worth it by that one phone call.

The couple dropped us off at the end of the road, and we ate our lunch at a little park before joining the Ōkura walkway. We got lucky with tides and were able to skirt the edges of the coast for this walk and very quickly found ourselves at Dacre Cottage. This was a gorgeous campsite with a shelter, toilets, water and some pretty nice, flat spaces to pitch tents. We were there early but the next kilometre or so involved a tidal crossing and it wasn’t low tide until 8pm. We would have to wait until the morning and cross at low tide.

Once again the TA fearmongering began. We had received videos from Sven who crossed a day or two before us showing everyone in their undies with the water up to their chests. I decided it would be fun even if it was meant to rain tomorrow. And besides, we all had indoor beds booked tomorrow night so it didn’t matter if all our stuff got soaked, right?

#8425. Never-Say-Die Climbers Will Try Everest Again This Weekend

Despite a forecast of high winds on November 21 and 22, Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have decided to begin a new attempt on the West Ridge of Everest on Sunday.

The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.

The forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend. Nevertheless, they will start up on Sunday, November 22, although that is the day with the strongest winds forecast.

“That day, we will remain low on the mountain and climb to our Camp 1 at 5,600m,” Sergey Kondrashkin wrote.  “From there, we will push upward when the weather improves and the winds die down, aiming to descend around November 28.”

This means the team does not intend to summit quite yet. The goal is to acclimatize by reaching 7,500m and then return to their headquarters in Lobuche.

“The question is, will we manage to complete the summit push within the time frame of our permit, which expires on December 15, and will the weather cooperate?” said Kondrashkin.

The fall season on Everest usually lasts until the end of November, since December 1 marks the start of Nepal’s winter climbing season. However, the permit dates may have been extended for this team, which is climbing off the normal route.

Once winter settles in, it will be the turn of Jost Kobusch of Germany, who will attempt to solo Everest in winter along the same route the Russians are now attempting.

On their third and latest trip up the mountain so far, the team only reached 6,700m before hurricane-force winds up to 130kph forced them down, according to former team member Natalyia Belyankina. Belyankina had to leave the expedition for health reasons but has stayed in touch with the others.

#8424. ‘Over the Moon.’ Ohio Hunter Shoots 215-Inch Buck from Her Favorite Stand on Her Birthday

Early Black Friday deals are here — Shop hunting gear, fishing tackle, optics, and more!

Published Nov 18, 2026 12:30 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Southeastern Ohio is known for its heavily wooded rolling hills and the big bucks that live there. Margaret Fuller of New Plymouth has hunted a small piece of private land there for years, and it’s where she was hunting this past weekend. In particular, she was looking for a giant 200-class buck she’d come to think of as “the Monarch.”

The big deer started showing up on trail camera about a month ago, although only at night. He was hitting scrapes near one of Fuller’s favorite ladder stands, and that’s where she hunted on Friday.

“It was bitter cold that day, but I hunted from the morning until noon,” Fuller tells Outdoor Life. “I went inside to get warm for a while, then went back out that afternoon and hunted until dark.”

That day she spotted a smaller buck about 50 yards from her stand. The deer was working along a trail toward her, but seemed to sense something was wrong and slipped away.

Fuller returned to that same stand the next day — her birthday — anyway. It’s the same spot she killed a 178-inch buck in 2022 during the firearms season.

“I didn’t get on stand until about noon,” says Fuller, a financial program manager for the Ohio Department of Natural Resources, “because I was so cold from the previous day’s hunt.”

About 3 p.m. she heard an ATV roaring on the neighbor’s property and she thought her hunt that afternoon was over.

“But a few minutes later I heard something in the woods, and then I caught a little movement,” says Fuller. “I stood up, grabbed my crossbow, and saw it was Monarch.”

He was at 50 yards and coming to a scrape along the same trail the little buck had walked the day before.

“I was worried the Monarch would spook, too, like the smaller buck did. I knew I had to shoot soon before he caught my wind.”

The buck began stopped to rub his rack on a tree, then started walking closer to Fuller.

“I knew I had to stop him before he got to the place where he could smell me, so I grunted,” says Fuller. “He stopped when I grunted, and I shot him at 30 yards.”

Instead of running, the buck dropped right there. Her shot had struck the spine, and the deer didn’t get up.

Fuller called her sons and husband, then climbed down from her ladder stand.

“I was on cloud nine,” she says. “I’ve been hunting deer since I was 14 with my dad, and I’d have given anything for him to have been with me and see this buck … And it was on my birthday, too!”

The family helped Fuller snap photos and field-dress the massive nontypical, which had 20 points. Then they butchered the deer at home.

The whitetail, which Fuller estimates is 5½ years old, was scored at 213 inches by Buckmasters measurer Toby Hughes.

“I’m over the moon,” says Fuller, who credits her success, in part, to “sticking with hunting even in the coldest weather.”

Read Next: Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Deer Hunting When the Weather Finally Turns Cold

She also adds that practicing meticulous scent control with her clothing and using a cover scent probably didn’t hurt, either.

“But the best thing is the joy of having my sons and husband involved in hunting. Everyone helped me and that family camaraderie is really special.”

#8421. Jost Kobusch to Train For Everest on Difficult, Dangerous Lhotse Shar

Jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22. His preparations include reaching 8,000m on a different peak.

Kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday. He spent the night at 6,000m, topped out again today, and went back down, as shown in his live tracker. He told ExplorersWeb that he will now rest for a few days in Lukla and then hike up the valley again to inspect conditions on his next acclimatization goal: the difficult Lhotse Shar (8,383m).

Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.

“My plan is not to summit but to tag 8,000m up its flank, before heading for Everest,” he said.

Lhotse Shar is one of the main points of the Lhotse ridge, and it is climbed from south side of the mountain, with Chukhung as the starting point. The main options are to climb the southeastern flank of the Shar itself or try a direct line up the formidable south face of Lhotse.

Neither of them is easy, and the upper sections are statistically dangerous. According to Wikipedia, Lhotse Shar has the highest fatality rate of all principal or secondary 8,000m peaks. For every two climbers who summit, one person dies attempting to.

Lhotse and its various points, as seen from the south. Graphic by Gorskie Mapy

The Austrian expedition that first reached the summit of Lhotse Shar (from the Southeast Ridge) in 1970 set four altitude camps, the uppermost at 7,600m. They used supplemental oxygen on their summit push. “Almost the whole of the route from below Camp 1 to Camp 3 was fixed with rope, as climbing was very difficult,” they reported in the AAJ.

Kobusch will not have to deal with the nearly vertical terrain and cornices near the summit, but will have to face difficult mixed terrain and uncertain conditions if he wants to venture up to 8,000m. He will not use bottled oxygen, and as far as we know, he will climb on his own.

Kobusch plans to reach the base of Everest on December 22 and solo the mountain in winter without oxygen, via the West Ridge — the same line currently being attempted by a Russian team.

This is Kobusch’s fourth attempt, and he is willing to try to reach the summit this time. However, when asked about it, he admits he does not know if such a feat is actually possible. “Every expedition, every training session, every difficult decision has been part of preparing myself for what I know will be the biggest challenge of my life,” he admits.

Kobusch’s is not the only confirmed climb this winter. Denis Urubko of Russia is reportedly preparing to climb Broad Peak in winter, possibly starting at the end of this year and continuing through January and February. On social media, Urubko mentioned he will be climbing with Vitaliy Skel. However, details of his route have not been confirmed.

Simone Moro of Italy has not decided whether to try Manaslu again this winter. He told ExplorersWeb he is still considering his plans while observing the “crazy weather this season.” Moro attempted Manaslu in fall to acclimatize and become familiar with the terrain. However, like every other team, he had to call off the attempt due to dangerous conditions following extremely heavy snowfall. Moro wants to climb the peak in alpine style.

#8418. From Icy Morning to Dead Phone — John Muir Trail Day 22

The night before I dropped down steeply from Donohue Pass.  In addition to the extra mileage, I also figured it would be warmer at that lower elevation.  The camping spot I selected, looking out at a huge golden, grassy meadow, was lovely.

Probably it was warmer there, but that did not mean it was warm!  It was already chilly when I went to sleep, and as the night went on it just got colder and colder.  I gradually added items to my sleeping bag — sleeping bag liner, long pants, long shirt, puffy hat, gloves — until I used up the entirety of my anti-cold arsenal.

Fortunately, that did the trick.  But had it been just a little colder, I would have been overwhelmed.  It created a cognitive conflict during my pee errands in the night.  My temperature sensors urged me to return to the tent as quickly as possible.  My spiritual-aesthetic soul urged me to spend just a little more time under the glorious blanket of moon and stars.

Towards morning, I had a bizarre dream.  It this alternate reality, I was having a hot affair with a woman.  Actually, it was a cold affair.  Why?  Because she was really an alien, part of an extraterrestrial race that was thinking of settling on earth, but who didn’t like our climate.  It was too hot for them.  Having superior technology, however, they were able to manipulate Earth climate and make it much colder to their liking.  So, I was freezing cold, despite having this torrid affair.

Another capability of the alien was that she could make you mostly forget what you had done the night before.  So, I kind of knew I was having the affair, but also wasn’t completely sure that I was.  The hilarious part was that the alien in the dream was my wife’s friend DG from middle school!  When I told Lee about the dream, I had to swear that I had never, ever contemplated having an affair with DG!

Did this moonlight view up through the tent inspire my strange dream?

When it began to get light, I gave myself a little bit of a break because it had been so cold.  My last trip outside the tent in the early dawn I looked out on that golden meadow and saw that it was all white, coated with icy rime.

By the time I took this picture, the rime was already melting, but some is still visible

I also retrieved my bear cannister; it too had a layer of ice on the top cover.

In close-up, the ice on the bear cannister is very visible

By this I knew it had gone below freezing during the night.  So, I allowed myself some extra minutes of warmth in the sleeping bag while I waited for the sun to rise above the lip of the mountains.

I finally got up at 6:30.  When the sun came up the temperature rose quickly, but the problem then was that the ice on my tent fly became moisture.  Also, the floor was pitched on a sort of pine needle-covered mud.  This was very comfortable, but it ended up sticking to my ground sheet.  It took some time and effort to get everything dry and clean.

After all the morning errands, I did not get on the road until – wait for it – ten a.m.!  On a short day, that might not have mattered, but I was planning another 17+ miles for this day.  The good news was, that I was camped in the Lyell Valley, and the mostly flat trail followed the Lyell Fork river for almost nine miles, all the way to Tuolumne Meadows.

Sometimes the river and trail were close like this, sometimes farther apart

With this cruisy route (and my late departure) I turned on the jets as I headed out.  With my unfortunate record of falling on easy trails, I was also trying to be careful.

A good portion of the trail, especially in the meadows, was indented into the earth.  My feet were below the ground level in a narrow track.  In this configuration, I find that hiking poles are more hazard than help.  So, for most of the first nine miles, I was carrying my poles rather than using them.

The statistics tell the tale.  Over those nine miles, I was only over 20 minutes (3 mph) twice.  My best mile I did in 17:49.  That is no record speed, but I don’t think I was even close to that pace anywhere else on the trail.

The scenery was interesting, but not spectacular.  The main thing, with this wide-open valley, was that I could measure my progress visually.  I could see an unusual-shaped mountain lining the valley up ahead; then after a time it was closer; then I was opposite to it; and then it was starting to fall behind me.  In a slower progression, I could see the distant mountains at the foot of the valley ahead (where the river changes direction).  At first, they were far distant, then middle distant, and eventually they were quite close.

The wide glacial valley, filled with meadows, and the mountains at the far end that grew larger as I got closer

At faster than 3 mph, I was in Tuolumne Meadows in under three hours.  As I got closer it was apparent there was a tourist center nearby.  Suddenly many more persons were on the trail and most of them were geared out for just a day of hiking or fishing.

The design of Tuolumne was a little weird, with a “downtown” road (Tioga Road) on the north side of the river and a hiking trail parallel on the south side.   I generally don’t love road-walking.  However, because the Wilderness Center (for permits) was in the middle of downtown, and because I wanted a permit to climb Half Dome the next day, I intended to go via the road.

NPS map of Tuolumne Meadows (in the lower right, I should have turned onto the “National Scenic Trail” but instead stayed on the John Muir Trail)

I missed the turn.  Maybe my feet just wanted to stay in the woods?  As I realized my error, I ran into a really nice couple who were staying at the fancy lodge nearby.  They had a map, and they confirmed, “Yeah, you just have to go back to that last turn and then turn to go across the river, instead of going straight.”

I had a sudden aversion to that plan, particularly because of the miles I wanted to hike that day.  The woman must have seen my expression, because she said, “My husband is just like you; he hates to backtrack!”

It was true.  So, I said, “Maybe I’ll go to the Visitor Center instead, and they can help me there.”  I continued on.

Now I was surrounded by roads and parking lots.  As I passed one lot, I saw a uniformed ranger manning the booth and I walked up to him.  When I explained what I wanted, he said, “First of all, to get a permit, you have to go to the Wilderness Center.  Second, they will not give you a permit to climb Half Dome.  The only way to get a Half Dome permit is to get a whole different multi-day permit that includes climbing Half Dome within it.”

Now that had not been my understanding, but he seemed very confident.  At this point I was even further away from the Wilderness Center and even less inclined to backtrack.  I could see my Half Dome ambitions evaporating.  I figured I could still go to the Visitor Center and give it one last try.

En route I saw that I would pass the market that hosted the famous Tuolumne Grill, and I realized that it was just about lunchtime.  I left my pack outside and went in to order.  It seemed a simple layout with some picnic tables outside to eat what you ordered.  I got a regular hamburger that came with orange juice and some wedge potatoes.  The juice tasted delicious on this now-hot day, and the wedges, slathered with ketchup, were good too.  But the hamburger?  It was an ordinary sort of dry hockey puck, not terrible, but not special at all.  I concluded the Grill was famous because of where it was, and not for what it served.

As I ate it all, I took my phone off of Airplane Mode and called my wife, Lee.  (I always hike with it in Airplane Mode to preserve my battery charge.)  When I told her the likely new plan, without Half Dome, she sounded excited that I was almost done.  I was looking forward to seeing her soon as well.

The Visitor Center was a mile-long road walk from there.  I had two animal encounters (of a sort) along the way.

First, I saw wild turkeys!  How funny to spend all that time in the wilderness without seeing any (though I did see grouse).  Then in congested Tuolumne I saw them.  I even got some pictures.

If not for the legs, the turkey blended in…

Second, as I was walking, a car slowed way down opposite me and the driver shouted out his window, “A bear just walked across the road up ahead less than five minutes ago!”

I shouted back, “Good!  I hope I see him, because I am getting really hungry!”

Whether he was pulling my leg, or he really saw the bear, I did not see any bear.  I was definitely looking out for it though.

After pine forest and silence, it was disconcerting to walk on asphalt with diesel engines roaring past me.  I was glad it was only a mile.  On arrival, I went up to the very nice woman in front of the Visitor Center and asked about permits.  No surprise, she directed me to the Wilderness Center.  I concluded the fates did not intend me to climb Half Dome.

Then I asked about getting out of Yosemite when I reached Happy Isles.  She explained about the free shuttle within the park that could get me to Curry Village from Happy Isles if I didn’t want to walk there.  From Curry Village, the YARTS (Yosemite Area Regional Transportation System) could transport me for a fee.  The end of their line was Merced, about three hours away.  I figured I could take a train or bus from Merced, or maybe Gabriel could come from Santa Rosa and pick me up there.

This lady pointed to the YARTS timetable on their bulletin board and suggested I take a picture of it.  I replied, “That’s a great idea!  You’re a lot smarter than I am to think of it!”

She also gave me a paper map of the Yosemite Valley to include Happy Isles and Curry Village, saying, “I know you hikers don’t like to add weight, but I think you might find this useful.”

I told her I was sure I would and stashed it away.

With that, I aimed for the trail, which passed a ways behind the Visitor Center.  It was a relief to be walking on pine needles again!

It is funny how quickly the crowds taper off as you get even a short distance away from the tourist centers.

The other big change was in elevation profile.  In the morning, the trail had ranged from flat to slightly downhill.  Now I would face climbing up past Cathedral Lakes to Cathedral Pass.  This was the last pass on the John Muir Trail.  It was about 9,700 feet which was a lot lower than the passes in the south, but still more than 1,000 feet above Tuolumne Meadows.

Perhaps it was my energy expenditure in the morning, but now I was puffing and panting as I ascended.  “Where is my juice?” I asked myself.  “This is as bad as climbing Cottonwood Pass on the first day of the JMT!”

I was breathing hard, but enjoying the enormous granite rock

The inspiration was the views.  There was more than one rocky shape that could qualify as a “cathedral.”  Imagine Notre Dame.  Imagine that the roof is one thousand feet high, the spires soar over 1,500 feet, and the nave stretch two miles.  Then imagine a landscape dotted with two or three of these behemoths.  It was magical.

About the time my legs finally got warmed up, I came across a couple that were on the first day of their John Muir Trail hike.  The reversal I had imagined, when encountering near-finishers at the start of my own hike, was coming true.  In chatting, he warned me, “Oh, there’s no water except at Upper Cathedral.”

I appreciated that intel and was on the lookout for a spot near Upper Cathedral Creek.  As I ascended, coming above the tree line, I was surprised not to find it. Then, as I passed a quarter mile from Upper Cathedral Lake, I saw some people emerge on a trail from the lake onto the main trail.  Suddenly it dawned on me that there was no creek.  He meant the lake!

It was late afternoon and I wanted to press on and find a campsite.  But if this was really “last water” it would be foolish not to take the detour for it.

The lake seemed to have mostly marshy and muddy access points.  These would entail wet feet and dirty water to filter.  However, I saw a rocky promontory jutting into the lake where a bunch of guys were hanging out.  I headed there to refill my water.

I began chatting with them and learned they were from Kansas City.  I asked them whether they lived in Kansas or Missouri and they said that only someone who knows Kansas City would ask that question.  I explained that I had a cousin who lived in K.C. and they told me they lived on the Kansas side.

Overall, they were nice enough, but the banter occasionally felt a little mocking.  For example, they asked me, “Did you go up Whitney?”   I replied that I had, but that I had been fighting a respiratory infection, making it very difficult.

They responded, “Oh, that just adds to your story about climbing Mount Whitney.  Like, ‘everybody else just climbed it, but I climbed it with a respiratory infection, coughing every step of the way!’”

They were actually not wrong, but the tone felt a little snarky.

After I filled both my water bottles and my Katadyn BeFree to have maximum water available, I headed back toward the trail.  One of the guys, maybe the leader, followed me a short distance and called me over.  He was asking me about the trail, and it turned out he had done the trail himself a few years before.  It seemed a little odd, but I took him as just wanting to reminisce a bit about his own experience.

In a quarter mile I was back at the junction with the JMT.  The beauty of the scenery around Cathedral Lakes is so inspiring, I wanted to take some more pictures.  John Muir himself said, on summiting Cathedral Peak, “This I may say is the first time I have been at church in California, led here at last, every door graciously opened for the poor lonely worshiper.”  (Quoted from My First Summer in the Sierra, Chapter 10, entry for September 7, 1869.)

So, this “lonely worshiper” reached for his smart phone to capture the majestic giants and discovered… nothing.  Nothing at all, a black screen.  Now my eyesight is not great without glasses, but I had thought my phone showed 65% of charge when last I checked.

In case it had just shut off for some reason, I tried to restart it, but still nothing.  I was crestfallen, thinking, “Oh no!  My phone died here on the trail with barely one day left on my hike!!!”

I could not fathom how it happened.  I had not dropped it that I could recall.  Deeply disappointed, I began having paranoid thoughts.  “If I had charge, and now suddenly I don’t, could that guy who followed me, to talk to me, have had some technology that fried my phone?  Like some super magnet or something?”

It seemed wildly implausible, but the coincidence – that it happened right after our exchange – seemed strange.

Then I calmed down somewhat.  I reminded myself of what was truly important,  “This trip is about the experience itself.  It is not ultimately about telling the story or capturing the pictures, it is about your lived experience.”

Seen through that prism my loss was minor and I settled down.   My wife and I always try to distinguish “disappointments” from “tragedies,” and this was clearly the former.

With the light turning to a mellow glow in the sky, I continued hiking.  Cathedral Pass was not much further.   It was unusual, in that the trail reached the pass, but did not descend from there down the other side.  Instead, it continued on, ascending further up the ridge of one of the mountainsides bordering the pass.

Now my lack of a phone was frustrating because I had lost my navigation device.  I was not sure how far I should ideally go before selecting a camp, remembering that I wanted to make miles to ensure I could finish on the following day.

The mountains answered that question for me.  As I continued higher, I came to a turn on the outstretched flank of the range.  Extending from the trail was a large flat spot, with visibility in all directions.  The ground was ideal for pitching a tent.  The views were magical in the waning light.  I thought, “I can go further, and shorten my day tomorrow.  Or I can camp tonight in the most beautiful spot in the Sierras.”  That decision was an easy one.

In Tuolumne I heard we were in for another icy night, and I was now at a higher elevation than I had been the night before.  So, I was expecting cold.  In fact, as the sun dropped behind the peaks, I could feel the chill almost immediately.

I started to pitch my tent, and maybe I was in too much of a hurry?  I love my Big Agnes TigerWall, but on this night, as I tried to get a pole into the slot, the pole snapped.  After the dead phone, this might have been a devastating blow.  But in this stunning location, on the last night I needed a tent, it did not phase me.  Besides, I had been carrying a seemingly useless stupid little tube for miles and miles, wondering why I bothered, and now I had my answer.  I slid the tube over the broken spot, taped it in place with surgical tape (though that might have been unnecessary), and reseated the pole in the slot.  Good as new?  Maybe not, but close enough.

Having pitched my tent, I just basked in the beauty of the location for a few minutes.  Then I soaked my food and found a spot for a cat hole and dug what was likely to be my last cat hole on the trail.  The cold soak did not take long, but the result was the opposite of the previous night’s dinner.  That food had not rehydrated fully but was wonderfully seasoned and tasted delicious.  This night the mashed potatoes and chicken hydrated easily, but they were totally bland.  They didn’t taste bad really, they just didn’t taste like anything at all!

Of course, mindful as always that this is fuel first and flavor second, I wolfed it all down.

With no phone, I was communicating with my family by Garmin.  That was so onerous, typing out everything, one letter at a time.  (On the trail I learned of an app that makes this easier, but I didn’t have either the app or a working phone.)  Gabriel seemed amenable to picking me up in Merced, and so I realized I needed to make big speed the next day to get to Happy Isles.  The 4:50 p.m. YARTS departure to Merced arrived by 8:30 p.m.  Even that would mean getting back to Santa Rosa by midnight, after all.  Our back and forth about this on the Garmin was practically in code, but I thought the plan was set.

Wrapping up my chores in deep twilight, I stored everything in my bear cannister and – why not? — I hooked my phone to the charger.

Before going to sleep, I decided to just take a peek at the phone.  What??  Yes!  Yes!!  My phone was charging!!!

I was elated and still baffled as to how it happened.  I could not be sure.  The best explanation I came up with was this:  First, without my glasses I had misread the charge level on the phone.  It did not have 65%, it must have had much less.  Second, after speaking with my wife from the restaurant at lunch, I must not have turned Airplane Mode back on, so that the phone drained far more quickly in the afternoon than it did in the morning.  That is my best guess.  Operator error.

The most beautiful campsite — taken under the stars, after my phone revived

Snuggled in my tent, I got gussied up, wearing all of my clothing in preparation for a second icy cold night.

My tent in the moonlight of the last night — repaired and welcoming (except for the mess inside!)

It boggled my mind to think that – most probably – I was wrapped in my sleeping bag for the last time this year.  The excitement of (hopefully) completing the trail the next day would normally have kept me wide awake.  But no.  I was just too tired and slept right away.

#8417. The Paradox of Seeking First Ascents in Western Nepal

Western Nepal has plenty of unclimbed 6,000m peaks, and Fredrik Strang of Sweden and Sindre Kolbjornsgard of Norway went there planning to climb one. In the end, they settled for a slightly lower but equally memorable experience. It showed again that adventure goes beyond first ascents.

What I remember most clearly about that narrow summit is not the grade, the exposure, or the possibility of being first. It is the silence. No helicopters. No voices from a fixed-rope queue. No machinery, no aircraft, no distant sound of a settlement. Only the two of us, a serrated horizon, and an unfamiliar feeling that the mountain had asked a question rather than supplied an answer.

Sindre Kolbjornsgard, left, and Fredrik Strang. Photo: Fredrik Strang

After 18 expeditions to 8,000’ers and witnessing the evolution (or devolution) of climbing on these peaks’ normal routes, Strang and his partner knew they wanted something different. Quoting Ed Viesturs, Strang said: “The point is to climb, not just to summit.” With that in mind, the climbers set four criteria for their objectives:

Several route options face the climbers’ base camp tent. Photo: Fredrik Strang

Strang noted that there are many unclimbed peaks left in Nepal, but they were looking for a compelling climb, not just a dull summit for the record. They finally found one that satisfied their criteria, but then, as with so many other teams in Nepal this fall, harsh weather put their original objective out of reach. Not to mention that traveling Western Nepal is anything but simple.

“Our intended destination was in the Nyalu Lek area north of Simikot,” Strang revealed. “We planned to cross Nyalu La, a pass around 5,000m, with a support party that included porters and pack animals.

“Getting from Surkhet to Simikot took two rough days by road, with landslides having damaged or obliterated sections of the route. At Simikot, we learned that Nyalu La was probably impassable. Even reaching the place where we planned to start trekking had been uncertain.”

When they did reach the area, they confirmed that their planned peak was not an option. Hiking further down the valley, they pitched their tent at Phendol Kermi Camp. Snow had covered the trails beyond, but they simply had no time or money to move to some other region in Nepal. Instead, they decided to explore whatever was close to their camp.

During their stay, they encountered Mick Fowler and Victor Saunders of the UK. Bad weather had likewise spoiled the British pair’s plan to attempt an unclimbed 6,000m peak farther east, known only as Peak 6010, according to Mount Everest Foundation.. This would have been their second attempt on that peak. Ironically, dry conditions spoiled their 2025 attempt. This time, too much snow forced them back. Read more on the British climbers’ adventure here:

On October 6, Strang and Kolbjornsgard made their first acclimatization climb on a 5,177m peak at 30°20′49.82″N, 82°03′54.82″E. They found no records of any previous ascent.

“From base camp, the mountain looked straightforward, and lower down, it largely was,” Strang recalls. “Steep grass, mud, and broken rock led toward the upper slopes. But at about 4,500m, the route disappeared beneath knee-deep snow, then waist-deep snow, and every step became a small excavation.”

In the following days, they scouted and flew their drone down side valleys, looking for possibilities. Their second peak was 5,227m in altitude, located at 30°07′50.86″N, 81°41′56.58″E. Again, there were no records of previous ascents. Parts of it were far from fun.

“Below 4,500m, progress was tolerable, but above that, we were back to forcing our way through knee-deep, sometimes chest-deep snow,” Strang wrote. “A tremendous amount of work for very little enjoyment.”

Luckily, the climb improved once they reached the summit ridge, on relatively easy mixed rock and ice, which they assessed at PD+.

“Fowler and Saunders climbed the mountain several days later and found an easier way to descend and reascend the step on its western side,” Strang noted. “Their solution was a reminder that the first line a team takes is not necessarily the best one.”

Still, the peak that most drew the climbers’ attention was a remarkable 5,337m tooth of rock above Yangchya Lake at approximately 30°07′09.36″N, 81°41′21.15″E.

“We began calling it Daara Peak — a name inspired by the Nepali word for a projecting tooth or fang and by the mountain’s striking shape,” Strang said. He notes that the name is provisional while they await a response from the authorities about their suggestion.

Strang describes the peak as “a saber-toothed tiger’s canine protruding from a mass of rock. The terminal pinnacle was about eight meters high, overhanging and sharply defined against the sky.”

The climbers about to reach what they called Daara Peak. Drone photo: Brizendra Bhattarai

The problem was approaching the peak in deep, heavy snow from Yangchya Lake. They failed on their first attempt to tackle its northeast headwall. After waiting out another snowy spell, the climbers returned for a second attempt on October 17-18.

The climbers dealt with 250m of rather poor rock, a complex approach to the headwall across a bergschrund with soft snow, and the uncertainty of moving on unfamiliar terrain. They had no idea of the difficulties ahead or whether they could protect the passages ahead on their way to the summit. The route included vertical granite walls, with cracks adequate for cams, some mixed terrain with the crux at M6, a steep couloir, and then the summit ridge: a granite edge with some 30cm of snow on top.

Climbing terrain on Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang

Rather than technical difficulty, the section was delicate due to exposure and a lack of comfortable belay stations. Yet, the climbers reached the summit on October 18, including the top of the final pinnacle, thanks to a crack in the rock.

Strang admits that the climbing details suggest a rather straightforward ascent: a 5,337m summit via its northeast side in five pitches with difficulties up to M6. However, Strang judges the climb on a different scale. “The technical crux was behind us, but it was the part I remember most vividly,” he explained. “It was the silence.”

Strang and Kolbjornsgard’s route up Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang

On many of the 8,000m peaks I have climbed, the human presence has become part of the landscape: camps, radio calls, fixed ropes, queues, and the distant sound of aircraft. Up here, none of that reached us. Mountains extended in every direction. There was no audience, no ceremony, no one to confirm that we had accomplished anything at all.

Strang also reflects on the paradox: They enjoyed the wild terrain but, if every climber chases solitude by visiting these last remote valleys, the character of these places will inevitably change. For Strang, the question is not to ban access. However, he says:

Perhaps some summits should remain untouched — not because we lack the skill or courage to reach them, but because future generations deserve to inherit mountains that have not all been reduced to objectives.

The climb from the ridge. Photo: Fredrik Strang
